Curriculum

National curriculum in English medium: a parent’s guide.

Children are learning subject knowledge and the language used to express that knowledge at the same time. Understanding this double task helps families offer the right kind of support.

By Princeway CollegePublished 6 November 20268 minute read

“English medium” describes the language through which subjects are taught. It does not mean that every child begins school already able to discuss mathematics, science or the world around them in confident English.

For many learners, the early years involve two connected journeys: understanding the concept and learning the English words, sentence patterns and classroom language needed to work with it. A thoughtful school plans for both.

The curriculum remains the learning map

When Sri Lanka’s national curriculum is taught in English medium, the expected areas of learning remain central. The medium changes how teachers explain, discuss and assess that content. Children must learn words such as compare, measure, observe and explain as well as the ideas behind them.

This is why simply memorising an English definition is not enough. A child may repeat a sentence accurately while still being unsure what it means. Good teaching moves between concrete experiences, pictures, spoken explanation, demonstration, reading and written practice.

Understanding comes before performance

Parents sometimes become concerned when a child can explain an idea informally but struggles to write it in English. The gap is important, but it does not always mean the concept is missing. The child may need help turning understanding into academic language.

Ask the child to show, draw or demonstrate the idea. Then help attach words to what they already know. For example, a child can first sort objects into groups, explain the reason in simple language and only then learn terms such as “properties” or “classification.”

Language should open the door to knowledge. It should not become a wall that hides what a child understands.

The hidden vocabulary of classroom tasks

Some words belong to a subject. Others appear in almost every subject: identify, describe, complete, underline, estimate, discuss and justify. A child can know the answer but lose marks because the instruction itself is unclear.

At home, notice these task words in homework. Instead of completing the exercise for the child, ask, “What is this question asking you to do?” Encourage the child to rephrase the instruction. This small habit develops independence and reveals where language support is needed.

Keep the home language strong

Families do not need to replace every home conversation with English. Rich conversation in a familiar language supports thinking, storytelling, relationships and general knowledge. A child who can discuss an idea clearly in one language has a foundation for learning how to express it in another.

Parents can read or discuss the same topic in more than one language, especially when the concept is new. What matters is that the child thinks actively rather than repeating sounds without meaning.

Useful support at home

  • Read for meaning: pause to predict, question and retell rather than only sounding out every word.
  • Build a small word bank: record a few useful subject words each week with a drawing or example.
  • Talk before writing: let the child say the answer, improve it together and then write it.
  • Use ordinary experiences: cooking, shopping, travel and household tasks provide natural mathematics, science and vocabulary.
  • Protect thinking time: a short pause before answering is not failure; the child may be organising language.

Look at progress from more than one angle

Test scores are one source of information, not the whole picture. Notice whether the child can follow instructions more independently, explain an answer with greater detail, read for longer, ask better questions or use new vocabulary in conversation.

When speaking with a teacher, ask separately about subject understanding and English expression. This leads to a clearer plan. A child may need more practice with a mathematical concept, more language for explaining it, or both.

Questions to ask an English-medium school

  • How is new vocabulary introduced and revisited?
  • How do teachers check understanding when a child is quiet?
  • How are reading and speaking developed across subjects?
  • What support is available when English limits a child’s ability to show knowledge?
  • How are families informed about progress in both content and language?
